progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C02 (acid + hydroxide → salt + water; acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂; magnesium hydroxide antacid equation; ammonium sulfate fertiliser; salt formulas from charges). C01 (Brønsted-Lowry: a base accepts a proton; carbonate is a proton acceptor; CaO + SO₃ shows an oxide reaction with no proton, the Brønsted-Lowry limit). Stage 5 (Years 9 and 10): pH scale as "lower is more acidic, seven neutral", balancing, states. Module 5: precipitation and Fe(OH)₃ as a brown precipitate (chem-m5-c13). Not assumed: pH calculation, strength.
progression.startsWith: Identify an acidic or basic problem in a real setting. The video opens: Four problems. Heartburn from stomach acid. A paddock where young wheat is stunted and yellow.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying the acidic problem in four settings and its cause; choosing a treatment using safety, cost, gentleness and products; writing CaCO₃ + 2HCl, CaCO₃ + 2H⁺, Ca(OH)₂ + SO₂ and H⁺ + OH⁻ equations with the precipitation step Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃; explaining each effect on pH and what is left behind; explaining how SO₂, an acidic oxide with no hydrogen of its own, is neutralised through the sulfurous acid it makes in water; explaining why mine water is treated with hydrated lime rather than limestone. No fertiliser manufacture (C02), no modelling media (chem-m6-c09), no strength (chem-m6-c05), no pH calculation (chem-m6-c07).
progression.nextLesson: why some acids are strong and others weak, and how that differs from concentration (route chem-m6-c05).

teaching.task: Stomachs, soils, chimneys and mine creeks can all suffer from too much acid. How do you choose a base to neutralise each one, and what does the reaction actually do?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) four problems, one root cause (too much acid), but sodium hydroxide fixes none of them: how do you choose? (1); (2) neutralising uses up the extra hydrogen ions; four questions choose the base (2); (3) stomach: NaOH caustic; antacids barely dissolve and react with the acid they meet; hydroxide gives salt and water, carbonate also CO₂ (3); (4) soil: leaching and ammonium fertiliser make it acidic; below about pH 5.5 aluminium dissolves and damages roots (4); (5) lime: carbonate accepts two H⁺ and breaks into water and CO₂; pH rises; aluminium returns to solids; limestone barely dissolves without acid, so it does not overshoot (5); (6) chimney: sulfur in coal burns to SO₂; in water droplets it makes sulfurous and sulfuric acid: acid rain (6); (7) scrubber: Ca(OH)₂ slurry plus SO₂ gives solid CaSO₃ and water; SO₂ is an acidic oxide with no hydrogen of its own, which makes sulfurous acid in the slurry water for the hydroxide to neutralise; solid collected, often made into gypsum (7); (8) mine drainage: exposed iron sulfide makes sulfuric acid and dissolved iron; harms river life directly and keeps metals dissolved (8); (9) hydrated lime: OH⁻ neutralises H⁺, and rising pH precipitates metal hydroxides as sludge; chosen over limestone because it acts faster and reaches the higher pH some metals need, so the dose is controlled; alkaline waste the other way (9); memory aid: every fix leaves something behind; problem, treatment, equation, effect (10); two attempts and brief feedback (11 to 14); decision rule and handoff (15); key notes (16).
teaching.conversationalApproach: four real problems share one cause, too much acid, and the hook asks why sodium hydroxide fixes none of them. Each setting is then a short case in the same order (the problem and its cause, the chosen base, the equation, what the reaction leaves behind), with the choice card lighting the criterion in use. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Four problems. Heartburn from stomach acid. A paddock where young wheat is stunted and yellow. A coal power station chimney. And a creek running orange below an old mine. Each one comes down to the same thing, too much acid, and each is fixed by neutralising it with a base. But you can't just pour sodium hydroxide into a stomach, a paddock or a river. So how do you choose the base, and what does the reaction actually do?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A lake has become acidic as a result of acid rain, and its fish population is declining. Powdered limestone is added to the lake. Explain how the limestone raises the pH of the lake water. Include a balanced equation in your answer." Transfer: the soil reaction moves to a lake, and the student must write the net equation and the cause of the pH rise. Crossed mistake: "Ca²⁺ ions neutralise the H⁺ ions" (site quick-check distractor A). (A2) "Some power stations remove sulfur dioxide from flue gas using powdered limestone, CaCO₃, instead of calcium hydroxide. The products are calcium sulfite and one gas. Write a balanced equation for this reaction, and identify one disadvantage of using limestone." Transfer: the scrubber equation with a carbonate instead of a hydroxide. Crossed mistake: "CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + H₂O".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate applications of neutralisation reactions in everyday life and industrial processes" four applications, each taught as a problem, a chosen treatment, an equation and an effect: antacids (everyday), liming acidic soil (agriculture), scrubbing sulfur dioxide from flue gas (industry) and treating acidic mine drainage (industry, with a one-sentence note that alkaline waste is neutralised the other way). Not here: making fertiliser salts (taught in C02 scene 8; recalled in one clause in scene 4 as a cause of soil acidity); particle-diagram and multi-representation modelling of neutralisation (the site's card 6 belongs to the dotpoint "model neutralisation of strong and weak acids and bases using a variety of media", route chem-m6-c09); strength (chem-m6-c05); antacid titration and back titration (chem-m6-c15); heat of neutralisation (chem-m6-c03); toothpaste and fluorapatite (fluoride's main role is not neutralisation; left out to keep one main question); the 1952 London smog history (its site claims need sources, see corrections). No pH calculations: pH is used only as "lower means more acidic, seven is neutral" (Year 11 and C02 litmus level; pH itself is chem-m6-c07).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: H⁺ teal token (C01); OH⁻ violet; carbonate violet outline; CO₂ grey-green bubbles; water pale blue; spectator and product metal ions amber; solids white or rust brown; the pH strip bar acid red to neutral green to base purple, with a white marker. Board layout (constant): the plate for the current setting large on the left; the right holds one thing at a time (the lens, or the equation strip with its tag); a slim "choice card" (four words: safe, cheap, gentle, leaves behind) sits small in the top-right corner from scene 2 onward and lights the word being used; the short question sits top-left in one line. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; tags fade when their sentence ends. Reuse: `m6-antacid-tablets-v1.png` (three white chalky tablets, one broken; scene 3, hook), `m6-flue-gas-scrubber-v1.png` (cutaway scrubber tower: dark smoke enters a duct at left, two banks of spray nozzles, milky slurry pool at the base with a pump, a white plume leaves the top; scenes 1, 6, 7, attempt 2 feedback), `m6-fertiliser-granules-v1.png` (scene 4 clause, small), `m5x-ppt-feoh3-brown-v1.png` (brown iron hydroxide precipitate; scene 9 callback), `m6-marble-chips-acid-v1.png` (scene 5, small, to show carbonate fizzing in acid as the same reaction as lime in soil), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (scene 3, coded label "hydrochloric acid, like stomach acid"). Not used: `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (inspected: white lime pouring from a metal scoop held by a human hand onto soil beside a seedling; the hand breaks the no-human-figures rule and cropping leaves a floating scoop; replaced by the new pair below). No human figures.
design.transitionPlan: The four setting plates open together, then each takes the large left slot in turn (stomach, paddock, chimney, creek) while the right holds the lens or the equation strip one at a time; the choice card sits in the top-right corner from scene 2 and lights the word in use; the pH strip marker moves as each treatment acts; the memory aid gathers what each fix leaves behind; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the question; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
